howto.name: How to find out what governs a data centre near you

steps.name: Check the city first
steps.text: Search the municipality website for a data centre FAQ, plus the operator name and terms like fuel cell, substation, rezoning, moratorium and ordinance. Where a city has had an argument about a campus it has usually published a page about it, and that page carries figures no operator publishes.

steps.name: Find out whether the city actually has jurisdiction
steps.text: Generation above a state threshold is usually reserved to a state siting board, and a local government cannot permit or condition a facility that holds a state certificate. In Ohio the threshold is 50 MW under Revised Code 4906.13(B). Check your state equivalent before assuming a council vote matters.

steps.name: Read the utility commission docket
steps.text: Large-load interconnection, rate cases and cost-allocation rulings are public. They tell you the capacity constraint, the timeline, and whether the commission has ruled on who pays.

steps.name: Read the air permit, not the press release
steps.text: A permit that sets no carbon dioxide limit is not the same as a facility that emits none. Where other regulated pollutants fall below federal thresholds, CO2 limits are often simply absent from the permit.

steps.name: Read the abatement agreement
steps.text: The term of the tax exemption and the term of the community payment are frequently different lengths. That arithmetic is public and is rarely stated side by side.

short: Every other framework on this site governs what an AI system may do. This one governs where it may physically exist. Five separate regimes decide that, none of them AI law: state power siting boards, municipal zoning, public utility commissions, environmental permitting, and pipeline thresholds. A city can lose the argument before it starts, and often does.
title: Data Centre Siting, Power and Local Regulation
subtitle: Who decides where AI compute gets built, and who pays for the electricity
body_html:
The one-paragraph answer

Data centre siting and power regulation is the body of law that decides where AI compute may physically be built and what it may draw from the grid. It is not AI law, and almost none of it mentions artificial intelligence. Five regimes do the work: state power siting boards, which in many states take exclusive jurisdiction over generation above a threshold; municipal zoning, which can permit or prohibit the building itself; public utility commissions, which decide interconnection and who bears the cost; environmental permitting, which sets what may be emitted; and pipeline and infrastructure thresholds, below which no approval is required at all. A city that objects to a project may find it has no standing to stop it, while a city that wants no more of them can close its zoning entirely. Both happened in 2026.

Why this is separate from every other framework here

The EU AI Act governs what a system may do. ISO 42001 governs how an organisation manages it. The NIST AI RMF governs how risk is assessed. None of them governs whether a 300 megawatt campus may be built beside a school, who pays to reinforce the transmission line, or whether the turbines running it need a carbon limit.

Those questions are answered by utility and land-use law that predates generative AI by decades, and they are now the binding constraint on AI capacity in several US states. A model that cannot be trained because the interconnection queue is full is as constrained as one blocked by statute.

The five regimes

1. State power siting boards

Most US states reserve approval of large generation to a state board rather than to local government. In Ohio, Revised Code section 4906.13(B) gives the Ohio Power Siting Board exclusive jurisdiction over generating facilities above 50 megawatts, and provides that no local government may require a permit or otherwise condition the construction and operation of a facility holding an OPSB certificate.

The practical effect is visible at Hilliard, Ohio, where AEP Ohio is building a 72.9 megawatt solid oxide fuel cell plant of 228 Bloom Energy units on Amazon Scioto Darby campus, approved by the board on 22 September 2025. The city asked AEP and Bloom to add carbon capture. It could ask; it could not require. Hilliard published its own explanation of why, which is unusually candid municipal writing and worth reading in the original.

2. Municipal zoning

Where a state has not pre-empted it, a city retains the ordinary land-use power to permit, condition or prohibit. On 5 March 2026 the City Council of Fayetteville, Georgia adopted Ordinance 26-O-12, amending chapters 200 and 400 of its Unified Development Ordinance to prohibit data centres in every zoning district in the city. Fayetteville already hosts a QTS campus of thirteen buildings and approximately 6.2 million square feet; the prohibition does not touch it, and closes the city to anything further.

That pairing is the clearest illustration available of how quickly the politics move. The same city that permitted 6.2 million square feet publishes, on the same website, the ordinance that will permit no more.

3. Public utility commissions

Commissions decide interconnection, rates and cost allocation, and they have begun to rule specifically on whether data centre load may be recovered from residential customers. On 31 July 2025 the Georgia Public Service Commission ordered a freeze of Georgia Power base rates through 2028, stating that while it continues work to prevent new data centres from shifting costs to residential customers, rates cannot increase.

The commissions are also where capacity constraints become visible before they become news. AEP stated at Hilliard that it did not have sufficient transmission capacity to serve all the planned buildings on a single campus, which is why the fuel cells are there at all.

4. Environmental permitting

An air permit governs what a facility may emit, but not necessarily everything it does emit. At Hilliard, the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency issued a permit containing no carbon dioxide limitation, because where a source emissions of other regulated pollutants such as particulates, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, ozone and lead fall below federally established thresholds, CO2 limits are not required to be included. The plant is projected to emit about 60,726 pounds of carbon dioxide an hour.

The city commissioned its own dispersion modelling rather than accept either side account. It found the plant would raise carbon dioxide by about 27.7 parts per million at the nearest home 800 feet away and about 3.6 parts per million at an elementary school 4,000 feet away, against an ambient 350 to 450 parts per million and a health threshold generally taken to begin near 5,000. A second independent review in May 2026 confirmed the method. That is what a locality doing its own work looks like.

5. Thresholds where no approval is required

Regulation frequently stops at a number. The natural gas pipeline feeding the Hilliard fuel cells is eight inches in diameter; the Ohio Power Siting Board does not require pre-installation approval for intrastate gas pipelines of nine inches or less serving a single customer, and PUCO does not require a pre-application. A significant piece of infrastructure can therefore be built with no dedicated approval process, not because anyone waived it, but because the threshold was drawn above it.

Tax abatement and what a community receives

Almost every large campus arrives with an incentive agreement, and the terms are public. Two examples from this registry, both stated by the municipality rather than estimated here.

Hilliard, Ohio holds a Community Reinvestment Act agreement with Amazon abating property tax on data centre buildings against a required investment of $200 million by 31 December 2026, which the city states Amazon has met or exceeded. Hilliard City School District receives up to $3.4 million a year: $400,000 plus $1.50 per square foot of building, against up to two million square feet planned.

Marysville, Ohio granted AWS a thirty-year, 100 percent property tax exemption on the assessed value of its two-building campus, against $15 million a year for fifteen years to the Marysville Exempted Village School District and the city. A thirty-year abatement against a fifteen-year payment is a common shape, and the arithmetic is rarely set out side by side.

Fayetteville, Georgia relays QTS project estimates of $150 million to $200 million a year in real property tax revenue and about $170 million in sales tax, supporting several hundred operational jobs. Those are operator projections relayed by a city, not assessed collections, and this site records them as such.

How to read a project near you

The single most useful source for any large campus is the municipality, not the operator. Cities that have had an argument about a project publish FAQs, commissioned studies, ordinances and council minutes, and those documents carry capacity figures, emissions figures, timelines and financial terms that no operator publishes. Three of the best records in this registry came from city websites in a single week.

Each facility page in the data centre registry carries what has been found for that site under headings for jurisdiction, the local record, and tax and incentives, with the source for each. Where a figure is absent, no source published it.

Four power numbers that are not the same number

Siting and utility documents use four different measures, and directories routinely print one as another. IT capacity is the load the computing equipment draws. Utility power capacity is the service the building may take from the grid. Standby generation is diesel plant that runs when the grid fails. On-site generation is dedicated plant such as fuel cells, which may serve the site behind the meter and export nothing. A facility described as 32 megawatts on a utility measure, 12 megawatts on a standby measure and 72.9 megawatts on a generation measure has not been described three ways: those are three different things.
